storm.summary_layperson: No storms are on radar over the cove right now, but the atmosphere to our west is expected to grow more unstable through the evening and a Severe Thunderstorm Watch is in effect for the NYC metro area until 9 PM — if a cell does organize and reach us, the cool Sound water should take some of the edge off it.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The marine layer (a pool of air cooled by the Sound that can choke storms as they cross it) holds a wide 12°F air–water gap now and stays above the protective 5°F threshold until about 9:48 PM — just past this window — but with nothing currently tracking toward the cove there's no storm yet to test it against.
storm.detail_html:
Radar (KOKX) shows no cells within range of the cove as of 3:35 PM, and there's no active NWS alert for Riverside specifically. But the wider picture is more active: the Storm Prediction Center has a slight-to-marginal severe risk over the area, and OKX has a Severe Thunderstorm Watch up for the western half of the region — including the NYC metro and Nassau County — until 9 PM. That watch does not currently cover Riverside/Greenwich, but it's close enough to watch closely as the evening goes on.

Locally, the marine layer — a shallow pool of air cooled by contact with the Sound, which can rob incoming storms of low-level instability as they cross the water — is moderate today: Sound water is 74°F against 86°F air, a 12°F gap. That gap should hold above the ~5°F threshold that matters for storm-choking through the entire 4–9 PM window, only crossing below it around 9:48 PM as the air cools after sunset. So any storm that reaches the cove before roughly 10 PM should still get some cooling benefit from the Sound.

The other side of the ledger is shear: HRRR has 0–6 km bulk shear in the mid-20s to mid-30s knots through the evening, briefly touching 36 kt around 4 PM while the sea breeze is still active — the classic setup for shear to organize and intensify a storm rather than let the marine layer choke it (a "punch-through" scenario). CAPE is currently modest (360 J/kg) but the model has it building to roughly 1,000–1,700 J/kg by 6–8 PM, which combined with 20+ kt shear crosses into the range where storms can organize well if anything fires.

Net call: with nothing on radar yet, the cove and its surroundings are in the same boat for now. If storms do develop and approach from the west or southwest across open water, expect the Sound to blunt them somewhat, especially before the marine layer fades near 10 PM. If they come from the north or northeast overland, or if CAPE spikes well past 1,500 J/kg with the shear already in place, that protection matters less and the cove sees the same risk as inland towns.

What would change the call: any radar echo showing up within 50 mi and closing, upgrade of the watch to include Riverside/Greenwich, or an upstream APRS station suddenly gusting hard. Recheck radar and the watch status before racing or working outside this evening.

wind.tactics_blurb: Fairly even pressure across the course on today's SSW–SW sea breeze, with a slight edge toward the east shore (Tod's Point side) near the mouth — start mid-line, play the oscillations, and expect the breeze to soften into patchy, drifter-ish conditions after about 8 PM.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Today is a sea breeze reinforced by the background wind (Regime A+): the air–water temperature difference (deltaT) is a strong 12.2°F, well above the ~5°F threshold needed for a thermal circulation, and the background gradient wind is itself light (about 6.4 kt averaged across airport-grade stations) and onshore from the south/southwest — so instead of fighting the sea breeze, it's topping it up. That combination means today should hold a bit longer into the evening than a pure-thermal day would.

Direction: current on-the-water readings (Riverside YC and the western-LIS station ensemble) already show S (190°), notably more veered than HRRR's own forecast (ESE 119°, corrected to SE 134° after applying the model's usual sea-breeze maturation adjustment) — a 71° model/obs gap. HRRR is under-resolving today's veer more than usual; the table above leads with the observed direction and lets it continue its typical clockwise drift toward SSW/SW through the afternoon rather than the model's lagging number.

Pressure across the course should be fairly uniform on this SSW–SW flow, with the geography table calling for slightly stronger pressure near the mouth and along the east shore (less shelter from Tod's Point) versus the west shore — a mild lean, not a big split. Start mid-line and don't overcommit to one side early.

Shift character: by mid-afternoon this sea breeze is past the "ramping" stage (that persistent-right-shift phase mostly matters before ~3 PM) and into a mature, oscillating regime — expect cyclical 10–20° shifts on a 5–15 minute cycle that reward playing each header rather than committing to one side of the course.

Speed-wise, 7–8 kt through the peak of the window is solid one-design dinghy racing (the "sweet spot" range), easing to 4–5 kt and patchy by 9 PM as the thermal engine shuts down near sunset (7:59 PM) and only the light background flow is left running the show — borderline drifter conditions by the end of the window, so don't expect the last race of the evening to look like the first.

data_caveats: 1 of 29 surface stations (GW4252, Old Greenwich) flagged as a temperature outlier and excluded from the ensemble.
